power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text:  Tracking children's vocabulary development in the language of instruction is of interest when classrooms are multilingual.
 Yet, few tests of receptive vocabulary have been specifically validated to function fairly over developmental time.
 A 50-item receptive vocabulary test drawn from local picture-and story books was validated.
 Items showed stable properties across three time points in one academic year.
The study provides a transferable template for fair tracking of vocabulary development in other similarly multilingual early childhood settings.
A strong oral language foundation is arguably the bedrock for learning in school.

A growing cross-national and cross-linguistic evidence base shows oral language to be an essential precursor to reading comprehension, with theoretical accounts converging on how language skills support comprehension processes (Perfetti et al., 2023; Snowling & Hulme, 2025).
text.formatted: A growing cross-national and cross-linguistic evidence base shows oral language to be an essential precursor to reading comprehension, with theoretical accounts converging on how language skills support comprehension processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Perfetti et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Snowling & Hulme, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, despite its critical role, there is limited tracking of children's developing language skills globally.

One reason for this imbalance may be the greater attention to, and investment in, tracking code-focused precursors to reading, such as reading fluency, compared to oral language skills, including vocabulary (Nag, 2016).
text.formatted: One reason for this imbalance may be the greater attention to, and investment in, tracking code-focused precursors to reading, such as reading fluency, compared to oral language skills, including vocabulary <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Nag, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The resulting neglect is problematic because, attainments in reading comprehension remain persistently low across multiple countries (PAL Network, 2025; see also Nakamura et al., 2023), compromising progress towards learning goals (e.g., United Nations, 2015 , 2025).
text.formatted: The resulting neglect is problematic because, attainments in reading comprehension remain persistently low across multiple countries (PAL <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Network, 2025</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Nakamura et al., 2023)</ref>, compromising progress towards learning goals (e.g., <ref type="bibr">United Nations, 2015</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A more sustained focus is needed on oral language assessments, their psychometrics, and approaches that allow meaningful comparison across languages and over developmental time.
Vocabulary knowledge offers a productive entry point for such work.

It accounts for individual differences in reading comprehension (Nation, 2018; Wagner & Meros, 2010) and is closely associated with broader oral language development (Frank et al., 2021; Giazitzidou et al., 2025; Massonnié et al., 2022), while also lending itself to efficient and reliable measurement.
text.formatted: It accounts for individual differences in reading comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Nation, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wagner & Meros, 2010)</ref> and is closely associated with broader oral language development <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Frank et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Giazitzidou et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Massonnié et al., 2022)</ref>, while also lending itself to efficient and reliable measurement.

text.text: Yet vocabulary assessment raises difficulties that are still underexamined: the psychometric stability of items over developmental time has received less scrutiny than their stability across demographic or linguistic groups (AERA et al., 2014; Embretson & Reise, 2000), and in addition, items adapted from established instruments may function differently across languages and across the exposure profiles that characterize multilingual development (Bialystok, 2017;  a Rasch-based validation of a contextually-situated Hindi receptive vocabulary test administered in a multilingual district in north India, considering item-level behavior across demographic, contextual, and developmental dimensions.

text.text: Children's word knowledge encompasses three interrelated components: vocabulary breadth, which refers to the number of words in the lexicon; vocabulary depth, which refers to the layers of meaning associated with those words; and morphological awareness, which refers to an understanding that words may be composed of smaller meaningful units.
Two bodies of evidence make a particularly strong case for greater investment in the assessment of these components.

The first concerns the relationship with early reading: attainments in vocabulary breadth and depth account for individual differences in reading comprehension, either directly or indirectly through their association with morphological awareness (e.g., Giazitzidou et al., 2025; Nation, 2013), so that tracking these component skills carries clear instructional relevance for both language and literacy development.

text.text: The second concerns the place of vocabulary within the broader oral language system.

Statistical modeling of relationships among component language skills shows that vocabulary knowledge is closely associated with the development of listening comprehension, grammatical knowledge, and narrative expression (Frank et al., 2021; Massonnié et al., 2022), such that assessing vocabulary provides insight into the developing language system as a whole.
text.formatted: Statistical modeling of relationships among component language skills shows that vocabulary knowledge is closely associated with the development of listening comprehension, grammatical knowledge, and narrative expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Frank et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Massonnié et al., 2022)</ref>, such that assessing vocabulary provides insight into the developing language system as a whole.

text.text: Taken together, these findings position vocabulary as both a core component of language and a practical point of focus for assessment, particularly when the aim is to capture variation in the language of instruction.

Tests of word knowledge may tap either receptive vocabulary, indexed by what is understood when hearing a word, or expressive vocabulary, indexed by what is produced in spoken or written form (Nation, 2013).
text.formatted: Tests of word knowledge may tap either receptive vocabulary, indexed by what is understood when hearing a word, or expressive vocabulary, indexed by what is produced in spoken or written form <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Nation, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Picture-based tasks are typical of the former, while definition tasks are typical of the latter.
In a picture-based receptive task, the child is presented with a small selection of images and indicates the picture that best matches a word spoken by the assessor.

Because the response demand is restricted to picture pointing, the task accesses the child's language system without taxing speech, reading or writing, a feature particularly advantageous in contexts where children have had limited opportunities for verbal expression or are shy.
Such formats are also straightforward to administer, making them especially suitable for multilingual contexts in which expressive demands and proficiency could vary considerably.
In addition, picture-pointing tests yield more reliable scoring than expressive tests (Dunn, 2019).
text.formatted: In addition, picture-pointing tests yield more reliable scoring than expressive tests <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dunn, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The seminal exemplar of receptive vocabulary assessment is the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT; Dunn, 1959), developed for Standard American English and subsequently adapted across multiple languages and contexts, with the current version organized by parts of speech and levels of lexical difficulty (Dunn, 2019).
text.formatted: The seminal exemplar of receptive vocabulary assessment is the Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test (PPVT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dunn, 1959)</ref>, developed for Standard American English and subsequently adapted across multiple languages and contexts, with the current version organized by parts of speech and levels of lexical difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Dunn, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A common approach to extending the PPVT to new linguistic contexts is direct translation, but words that appear equivalent across languages may differ in frequency, familiarity, or semantic range, leading to imprecision in ability estimation and reduced comparability across contexts; cross-national adaptations have shown substantial proportions of items with poor fit in translated versions (Leon & Singh, 2017).

text.text: Alternative approaches to item development include common conceptual cores such as the Swadesh lists, the THINGS+ dataset, and the LITMUS-CLT lists of picturable nouns and verbs (Haman et al., 2015; Stoinski et al., 2024; Swadesh, 1971), age-of-acquisition norms (Dulay et al., 2026; Łuniewska et al., 2016), and tailor-made lists grounded in local language use.

text.text: A twenty-year review identified 63 vocabulary assessments, of which 50 used picture-based formats across a wide range of language families, drawing variably on translated, common-core, and bespoke, contextually situated word lists (Nag, 2016).

text.text: More recently, Rasch modeling has been used to develop new receptive vocabulary tests for multilingual primary school populations, demonstrating the value of iterative psychometric validation in achieving appropriate itemperson targeting (Morea et al., 2024).

text.text: Together, these approaches highlight a central tension between cross-linguistic comparability and sensitivity to local language use-a tension particularly pronounced in multilingual contexts, where differences in exposure and language structure may influence how items function (e.g., Hoff et al., 2012).

text.text: Establishing that a vocabulary test is fit for purpose requires evidence across several psychometric dimensions: that items span the ability range of the target population, that the test yields reliable ability estimates, and that individual items behave as expected under a measurement model.
Recent Rasch-based validations have demonstrated that these standards are achievable for oral language instruments designed for young children.

For English, Hulme et al. (2024) reported excellent reliability, good model fit, and well-calibrated item difficulty, and for French, German, and Spanish, Morea et al. (2024) showed that iterative Rasch validation can achieve appropriate item-person targeting.

text.text: Few tests of receptive vocabulary, however, have been validated to function fairly over developmental time, a requirement implicit in efforts to track learning.

In addition, in multilingual settings where children bring diverse home languages and varying degrees of exposure to the language of assessment, the requirement for bias evaluation becomes especially pronounced.

Items that systematically favor one group over another compromise validity (AERA et al., 2014; Camilli, 2016), and within an item response theory framework this concern is formalized as measurement invariance-the requirement that item difficulty remain stable across groups and over time, so that differences in observed performance reflect differences in underlying ability rather than artefacts of measurement (Chen et al., 2025; Embretson & Reise, 2000; Rasch, 1980).

text.text: Three dimensions of invariance are particularly relevant to this paper.
First, sex differences in language performance are well documented in the early childhood years.

Girls tend to outperform boys on vocabulary measures from infancy through the school years (Eriksson et al., 2012; Petersen, 2018), and at the item level, knowledge of particular words may differ by sex as a consequence of differential socialization and activity contexts (Coffey et al., 2025; Kachergis et al., 2023).

text.text: If individual items systematically favor one sex, the test may yield biased ability estimates even when overall scores appear comparable.

However, sex differences go beyond language attainments and the direction of any bias is not fixed: globally, girls are more often disadvantaged in early-grade attainments, but opportunity structures in some contexts may produce the reverse pattern with more boys with lower reading attainments (Nag et al., 2014; UNESCO, 2025).

text.text: Second, when the language of assessment is not the child's home language, item functioning may be influenced by the degree of structural similarity between the two languages.

Cognate relationships, phonological overlap, and shared morphological patterns can facilitate performance for some language groups but not others (Bosma et al., 2019; Goriot et al., 2021), and direct translations of established instruments frequently produce substantial proportions of misfitting items (Leon & Singh, 2017).

text.text: Beyond individual language profiles, ambient exposure to the target language represents a further source of variation.

Traditional indices focus on parental language use and neighborhood exposure (DeAnda et al., 2016; Lindgren & Muñoz, 2013), but child-peer interactions are an understudied yet potentially influential source of language input.

text.text: Third, a requirement for any assessment intended to track development over time is that item parameters remain stable across assessment points-that is, the relative difficulty of items should not shift as children acquire new vocabulary (Millsap, 2010 (Millsap, , 2011)).

text.text: If items show differential functioning across time, the meaning of change scores becomes ambiguous: an apparent gain may partly reflect changes in how items function rather than genuine growth in ability.

Despite the importance of this requirement, temporal measurement invariance has received considerably less empirical attention than cross-group invariance in the vocabulary assessment literature, and we are not aware of any study that has explicitly examined item parameter stability over developmental time in a receptive vocabulary test for young multilingual children.
A further psychometric consideration specific to picture-based vocabulary tests is the multiple-choice format itself.
When items present four response options, children who lack knowledge of the target word have a non-trivial probability of selecting the correct picture by chance.

Within item response theory (IRT), the three-parameter logistic (3PL) model explicitly accommodates guessing through a lower-asymptote parameter, but its estimation demands large samples per item and yields parameters that do not lend themselves to straightforward applied interpretation.

For assessments intended to inform group-level research and tracking applications through total scores-the potential use case in child language research and educational settingsthe parsimony of the Rasch model offers a pragmatic advantage: a single difficulty parameter per item and direct interpretability of item-person targeting.
The trade-off is that violations of model assumptions, including guessing, are not absorbed into the model but instead surface as misfit.

A diagnostic strategy that pairs Rasch modeling with post hoc examination of item characteristic curves and multinomial distractor analysis can identify items affected by guessing or distractor interference, yielding actionable guidance for item revision without sacrificing the interpretive simplicity that applied use requires (Andrich et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2019; Thissen et al., 1989).

text.text: We examine how well a contextually situated test for receptive vocabulary captures variation in the language of instruction within a multilingual setting.

Specifically, we evaluate the Picture Test for Receptive Vocabulary (TalkTogether -Hindi; PTRV[TT-Hin]), a subtest of the Sanjhe Bol Child Language and Foundation Learning Assessment Battery, designed for children aged 4 to 7 years.
The assessment is administered in a multilingual district in north India, providing an opportunity to examine test performance under conditions of substantial linguistic diversity.

Using a Rasch modeling framework, we address four research questions: (1) To what extent does the PTRV(TT-Hin) yield reliable ability estimates and provide adequate coverage of the proficiency range represented in a linguistically diverse sample?
(2) Do individual items conform to the expectations of the Rasch model, and what patterns characterize items whose empirical response functions deviate from model expectations?
(3) Is item functioning invariant across sex, home language background, and level of peer exposure to Hindi?
(4) Are item parameters stable across three assessment points spanning one academic year, as required for the valid tracking of vocabulary development over time?
>Method
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Method</head>

text.text: The study was conducted in the final year of pre-school and Grade 1 in Hindi-medium public schools (locally called Balvatika and government schools) in Sirsa district in north India.

Children aged four to nine years (age at Time 1: M = 71.15 months, SD = 15.56; Mdn = 68 months) from 40 schools completed the test on three occasions at four-month intervals across one academic year (2023-2024).
Recruitment was with permission of the government department for school education.
Forty schools were randomly selected from the list of all schools managed by the government that already had seven or more children in target classrooms at the start of the academic year.
Sample sizes were 756 at Time 1, 841 at Time 2, and 352 at Time 3.
The variation in sample size across assessment points reflects continued school enrolment between Time 1 and Time 2, and reduced sample size at Time 3 to accommodate upcoming school closures.
The wide age range reflects an admission policy of first enrolment of out-of-school and newly arrived children to Grade 1.
The analytic sample for this paper comprised 1,949 test performances on the PTRV(TT-Hin).
Girls constituted 47.22%, 46.97%, and 48.58% of the sample at Times 1, 2, and 3, respectively.
Approximately one-third (32.6%) of participating children reported speaking two or more languages at home.
Hindi was one of the home languages for 69.18%, 51.72%, and 59.37% of children at Times 1, 2, and 3, respectively.
For children without Hindi in the home, languages spoken included Haryanvi, Bihari, Punjabi, and Wagdi-ordered here from greater to lesser linguistic proximity to Standard Hindi.
Some schools enrolled a higher proportion of Hindispeaking children, resulting in differing levels of Hindi exposure through peer interactions inside and outside the classroom.
At Times 1, 2, and 3, peer exposure to Hindi was high for 57.80%, 57.91%, and 63.35% of children, respectively.
Ethical approval for this study was granted by the Education Departmental Research Ethics Committee (DREC), University of Oxford (reference number EDUC_C1A_23_233), and
The Promise Foundation, India (reference number 11-11-2021).
Parents or guardians could opt out of children's participation in the assessment.

Opt-out was chosen because the focus on oral language aligned with the pre/primary school curriculum, with the centrality of oral language evident from daily scheduled lessons across the state and a teacher professional development training priority for the academic year.

Two sources informed the development of the preliminary word list: the Swadesh list (1971), and a Hindi child-directed print corpus of 38,133 sentences from 1,243 records spanning different genres and appearing in 236 books for 3-to-10-year-olds (Nag et al., 2025).

text.text: We focused on nouns, verbs, and adjectives.

For each word item, two distractors were (a) semantically close to the correct answer (close in definition and hence most plausible if unsure), and (b) phonologically close (overlap at word-beginning sounds or endings, and hence confusable).
The third distractor was semantically distant (loosely linked to the correct answer).

This procedure is arguably more rigorous than approaches that leave one distractor unconstrained (completely a random unit), since such options quickly fall out of the test-taker's decision-making process.
Each item was presented alone and contained four full-color pictures with the target and distractor pictures placed randomly on a quadrant.
A pre-pilot informed improvements to picture clarity and distractor quality (see SDM 1 in the Supplemental Digital Materials for issues resolved at this stage).
The final 50-item word list comprised 27 nouns, 20 verbs, and 3 adjectives, covering content categories like actions, nature, and describing words.
For exemplar items, including the target word and related distractors, see Table 1.

text.text: In addition to vocabulary performance, information was collected on each child's sex and home language (whether Hindi was one of the child's home languages).
Peer exposure to Hindi was computed using school-level data (the proportion of Hindi-speaking children in the child's school).
The test was administered in two sessions of 25 items each, which were ordered by difficulty based on estimates from the pilot study (for a brief report on item-level considerations see SDM 2).
Sessions were held on consecutive days or within the working week, depending on the school timetable.
Items were presented in one session using a standard laptop screen with display and recording using the Qualtrics platform, and using a paper-and-pencil format in another session.

The two options of online and offline presentation were initially considered anticipating poor internet connectivity in remote locations across the district, with the Qualtrics set also available as paper-and-pencil material.
In the end, connectivity issues disrupted 0.56% of online sessions (7 sessions at T1, 4 at T2, none at T3); these administrations were completed offline.
Testing was in a quiet location provided by the school.
Instructions to the child were to prompt picture pointing ("I will say a word.
Please show me the picture.").
The sessions began with two practice items.
A discontinuation rule of six consecutive incorrect responses was applied per session.
Assessor training was through role plays and practice sessions with four-to seven-year-olds, using audio recordings for skills audit (see SDM 3 for training materials).
Analyses were conducted within a Rasch modeling framework to examine reliability, item characteristics, and measurement invariance.
Given the task's scoring structure, the data were analyzed using a dichotomous Rasch model, with parameters estimated via marginal maximum likelihood (MML).
Score reliability was evaluated using Cronbach's α and Rasch person separation reliability, computed by pooling all time points into a single dataset.

Item difficulty estimates were reviewed across the ability continuum, and item fit was assessed using infit and outfit statistics (with values between 0.8 and 1.2 indicating good fit) and the correspondence between the model and empirical item characteristic curves (ICCs).
To evaluate distractor functioning across the ability continuum, a semi-parametric approach was used to estimate option characteristic curves for each multiple-choice item.

A multinomial logistic regression was fitted with response option (1-4) as the outcome and Rasch person ability (θ) estimate as the predictor, modeled using a natural cubic spline with three degrees of freedom.
This approach was used for descriptive and diagnostic purposes and does not impose the parametric constraints of standard IRT category models.
It allows visualization of how the probability of selecting each response option varies across ability and provides a flexible complement to the Rasch model.

This is consistent with nonparametric and semi-parametric approaches to item response modeling that estimate option characteristic curves without assuming a specific functional form (e.g., Mazza et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This is consistent with nonparametric and semi-parametric approaches to item response modeling that estimate option characteristic curves without assuming a specific functional form (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Mazza et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The resulting curves were used to identify potential violations of Rasch model assumptions, such as non-monotonicity in the correct response or irregular distractor behavior across ability levels.
Finally, measurement invariance was assessed by examining both uniform and nonuniform differential item functioning (DIF) via a logistic regression approach.
DIF was evaluated across sex, Hindi as a home language, peer exposure to Hindi, and pairwise time points (T1-T2, T2-T3, T1-T3).
All analyses were conducted in R, with full details including package and version details provided in the Supplemental Digital Materials (SDM 4).

text.text: Overall, the PTRV(TT-Hin) demonstrated good internal consistency (α = .82) and person separation reliability (PSR = .78).

Mean scores fell around the middle of the possible range at each time point, and no subgroup approached the floor or ceiling of the test, providing initial evidence of appropriate targeting across the linguistic and demographic profiles represented in the sample.

text.text: No item exhibited DIF by sex.
Two items showed statistically significant DIF by home language: Item 1 (seed) and Item 23 (treatment), both with small to negligible effect sizes (classification A).
Four items showed statistically significant DIF by peer exposure to Hindi: Items 1, 35 (to throw), 41 (rose), and 47 (to dig), again all with small to negligible effect sizes.

Notably, Item 1 was the only item to exhibit DIF across more than one factor, showing statistically significant effects for both home language and peer exposure, albeit both of small to negligible magnitude.
With respect to measurement invariance across time, multiple items exhibited uniform DIF in the T1-T2 and T1-T3 comparisons (see Table 4, final column).

text.text: Fewer items were identified as exhibiting DIF in the T2-T3 comparison, with two instances of non-uniform DIF (Items 16 and 38).
Most flagged items demonstrated small to negligible effect sizes.
Two exceptions reached moderate magnitude: Item 30 (sticks/logs) in the T1-T2 comparison and Item 46 (to hear/listen) in the T1-T3 comparison (for item functioning of all 50 items see SDM 7).
In summary, item properties remained stable across time, an essential requirement for a fair assessment in early childhood of developing receptive vocabulary in the language of instruction.
The aim of this study was to examine the tracking of receptive vocabulary over developmental time and across diverse linguistic experiences.

The PTRV(TT-Hin), a picture-based test of Hindi receptive vocabulary, was evaluated to see if it can serve as a fair and reliable tool for tracking early vocabulary development across the diverse early childhood linguistic profiles found in multilingual north Indian classrooms.
Such tracking is particularly relevant in contexts where low pace of learning has substantial downstream effects on educational attainments.
Using a Rasch modeling framework, we examined reliability, targeting, item fit, and measurement invariance across demographic, contextual, and developmental dimensions.
Taken together, the findings indicate that the instrument meets the core requirements for a vocabulary tracking tool in this context.

Two qualifications merit attention: a small subset of items showed misfit attributable to a combination of guessing, distractor effects, and-for two items-lower discrimination than the Rasch model assumes, and a small number of items exhibited differential functioning across assessment time points, though effects were predominantly small to negligible in magnitude.

At the test level, the PTRV(TT-Hin) demonstrated good internal consistency and reliability, meeting the threshold typically recommended for group-level research and tracking applications (Revelle & Zinbarg, 2009).

text.text: Examination of item-person targeting revealed a good spread of person ability estimates in approximate alignment with the item difficulty distribution, with no evidence of floor or ceiling effects across any of the three assessment points.
This is notable given the linguistic diversity of the sample, which ranged from children with Hindi as a dominant home language to those encountering it formally for the first time in school.

That the test captured variation across this proficiency range suggests that the contextually situated construction approach-drawing on both the Swadesh list (Swadesh, 1971) and a child-directed Hindi print corpus (Nag et al., 2025)-produced a set of items appropriately matched to the breadth of early vocabulary knowledge present in this multilingual setting.

text.text: Five of the 50 items were flagged through inspection of item characteristic curves, and one further item (Item 43) exceeded the statistical fit criterion, yielding six items with some form of misfit-a proportion consistent with expectations for a newly developed 50-item instrument.

The contrast between the well-fitting items (Figure 2) and the misfitting items (Figure 3) was instructive: where the well-fitting items showed close alignment between the empirical ICC and Rasch model expectation, with monotonically declining distractors, the misfitting items showed systematic departures attributable to two distinguishable mechanisms.

text.text: The first was guessing, observed in all five ICC-flagged items but most pronounced for the more difficult items (Items 42 and 49): an expected artefact of the four-alternative forced-choice format in which children selecting among pictures have a non-trivial probability of a correct response even when guessing (Andrich et al., 2016; Embretson & Reise, 2000; Jin et al., 2022).

text.text: The second pattern, evident for Items 12 and 47, was reduced item discrimination, possibly because the target words occupied a narrower band of familiarity or because the pictorial stimuli did not clearly distinguish the target from children's everyday visual experience of the concept.
The multinomial response probability curves provided diagnostic insight into the mechanisms underlying misfit.

Distractor interference-particularly from phonologically or semantically proximate options-contributed to the specific profiles of deviation for Items 4 and 42, suggesting that misfit was not simply uninformed guessing but reflected partial lexical knowledge: children with some familiarity with a word may have been able to eliminate one or two distractors without reliably identifying the target (Ludewig et al., 2023).

text.text: Item 43, the only item exceeding the statistical fit criterion, showed a distinct pattern of response unpredictability rather than systematic guessing or reduced discrimination, possibly reflecting pictorial ambiguity or polysemy of the target word.
Together, these six items constitute a tractable revision target.

The response probability data provide item-level diagnostic guidance: for the guessing-affected items, replacing proximate distractors with more clearly differentiated alternatives may reduce distractor-driven misfit; for Items 12 and 47, review of image clarity or conceptual distinctiveness is warranted; and for Item 43, review of the pictorial stimuli is indicated.
Perhaps the most substantively important finding for the validity of the instrument is the near-complete absence of non-negligible DIF across sex, home language, and peer exposure to Hindi.

No item exhibited DIF by sex even though a female advantage in language performance is a robust finding across languages and cultural contexts (Eriksson et al., 2012; Petersen, 2018), and its absence at the item level here indicates that the content and format of the PTRV(TT-Hin) do not systematically favor either sex.

text.text: Two items showed statistically significant DIF by home language, though both effects were small to negligible in magnitude.

Given that the sample included children from several distinct home language backgrounds-Haryanvi, Bihari, Punjabi, and Wagdi, differing in their structural proximity to Hindi-the near-absence of substantive DIF across these groups is notable.

This stands in contrast to findings from translated instruments, where substantial DIF is a common outcome (Chen et al., 2025; Goriot et al., 2021; Leon & Singh, 2017), and supports the case for locally grounded item development over direct translation.

text.text: Extending beyond individual language profiles, one characteristic of a multilingual setting is the extent of exposure to a target language that children can gain through their peer group in class.
Our study is the first to acknowledge peer-level exposure, quantifying this as a differential item functioning variable.

Four items showed statistically significant DIF by peer exposure, but all effects were small to negligible in magnitude, and no pattern of systematic peer-exposure-related DIF was apparent across the full item set.
Together, these results indicate that the PTRV(TT-Hin) calibrates ability in a way that reflects genuine variation in Hindi receptive vocabulary rather than artefacts of group membership.

A distinct and relatively underexamined validity question in language assessment concerns whether item parameters remain stable as children develop-a requirement for assessments intended to track longitudinal change (Millsap, 2010 (Millsap, , 2011)).

text.text: Most statistically flagged items showed small to negligible DIF across all three pairwise time comparisons, indicating that their difficulty ordering was maintained across one academic year of development and instruction.
Two items reached moderate effect sizes: Item 30 in the T1-T2 comparison and Item 46 in the T1-T3 comparison.

These shifts in relative item difficulty are interpretable as reflecting differential rates of acquisition for specific words across the proficiency range, rather than systematic measurement failure, but they warrant monitoring in future administrations.

Two further items showed non-uniform DIF in the T2-T3 comparison (Items 16 and 38), indicating a change in item discrimination rather than difficulty alone; this pattern may be consistent with increasing differentiation in word knowledge as children progress through the school year.

Taken as a whole, these findings suggest that the PTRV(TT-Hin) functions with sufficient developmental stability for longitudinal tracking within the one-year window examined here and adds to the limited but growing evidence base on item parameter stability in developmental and multilingual assessment (Millsap, 2010; Park et al., 2025).

text.text: The validation findings carry implications beyond the specific instrument examined here.

While it is well established that a picture-based receptive vocabulary test can be administered without literacy or expressive language demands, the PTRV(TT-Hin) demonstrates that a test built from locally relevant child-directed corpora can achieve the psychometric properties required for tracking early language development across a linguistically diverse sample.

The absence of systematic DIF across a wide range of home language backgrounds lends support to the view that bespoke construction-calibrated to local language use rather than adapted from instruments developed for other linguistic contexts-offers a more measurement-invariant approach than translation (Leon & Singh, 2017).

text.text: The test's efficient administration format and objective scoring are also relevant considerations for assessment at scale in low-and middleincome country contexts, where assessor training resources may be limited (Nag, 2016; Nakamura et al., 2023).

text.text: More broadly, the findings reinforce the value of receptive vocabulary as an assessment target in multilingual settings: picture-pointing tasks access the developing lexical system without taxing speech, reading, or writing, providing a window into oral language development that is particularly informative where children's proficiency in the language of instruction is highly variable (DeAnda et al., 2016; Frank et al., 2021).

text.text: Questions of generalizability arise at two levels.

At the sample level, the children in this study attended public schools in a single multilingual district in north India, and the home languages represented-Haryanvi, Bihari, Punjabi, and Wagdi-are all Indo-Aryan languages with varying structural proximity to Hindi.

It is not known whether the near-absence of DIF by home language would hold in early childhood settings involving typologically more distant language pairings, or whether the psychometric properties observed here would extend to private-school populations with different socioeconomic and language exposure profiles.
At the methodological level, however, the approach demonstrated here is designed to be transferable.

Several limitations bear on the interpretation of these findings.

The tracking window covers only one academic year, and it is not known whether the developmental stability of item parameters observed here would persist over a longer period, or whether items showing moderate DIF by time would accumulate larger effects with further follow-up.

In addition, the demographic variables were analyzed independently, and the study did not examine intersectional profiles-for example, girls from non-Hindi-speaking homes with low peer exposure-for whom the convergence of multiple factors may bear on vocabulary development in ways not captured by single-variable DIF analyses.

The observation that Item 1 was the only item to exhibit DIF across both home language and peer exposure suggests that cross-factor item behavior warrants further investigation, particularly given that home language background and peer exposure are themselves correlated in this sample.
Finally, the PTRV(TT-Hin) measures receptive vocabulary only.
A more complete account of lexical development would additionally require expressive measures capturing productive vocabulary knowledge and morphological awareness (DeAnda et al., 2016).

The item-level response data from the present study-including the multinomial response probability curves-offer a foundation for targeted revision of the misfitting items, and corpus-based resources such as child-directed print corpora (Nag et al., 2025) and age-of-acquisition norms (Dulay et al., 2026) provide candidate tools for selecting replacement distractors in languages for which psycholinguistic databases are not yet available.

text.text: The novel use of peer-level Hindi exposure as a DIF variable also merits further investigation; more granular indexing of peer exposure-for instance, the proportion of classroom instructional time in Hindi, or network-level measures of language use among peersmay reveal threshold or interaction effects not detectable with the binary grouping variable employed here.

Finally, the construction approach demonstrated in this study is exportable: applying it to other languages of instruction in multilingual contexts, such as in South Asia, would allow examination of whether item difficulty orderings transfer across typologically related languages, extending the evidence base for cross-linguistically comparable vocabulary assessment (e.g., Frank et al., 2021).

text.text: Receptive vocabulary, what is understood when hearing a word, underpins both developing reading comprehension and wider learning.

The PTRV(TT-Hin) meets the requirements for a vocabulary tracking instrument for monitoring Hindi receptive vocabulary development in multilingual north Indian classrooms: adequate reliability, well-calibrated targeting across a wide proficiency range, and a largely small to negligible pattern of differential item functioning across sex, home language background, peer exposure, and developmental time.
The misfit observed in a small number of items is diagnostically interpretable and constitutes a tractable agenda for instrument refinement.

Taken together, this study also offers a methodological template-combining Rasch analysis, DIF evaluation, and multinomial distractor modeling-for developing and validating vocabulary assessments in other early childhood multilingual settings where contextually appropriate language tracking tools are both urgent and underdeveloped.
Such fair tools to track children's oral language skills in the language of school instruction are of interest to both intervention research and mainstream language testing.
